Title: Mid‐Infrared Reflectance Modulator Based on a Graphene CMOS‐Compatible Metasurface
Text:
RESEARCH ARTICLE
www.lpr-journal.org
Mid-Infrared Reﬂectance Modulator Based on a Graphene
CMOS-Compatible Metasurface
Fei Han, Kacper Pilarczyk, Zaoyang Lin, Conglin Sun, Guy A. E. Vandenbosch, Joris Van de
Vondel, Pol Van Dorpe, Xuezhi Zheng,* Niels Verellen, and Ewald Janssens*
Optical modulators based on tunable graphene-metal hybrid metasurfaces
have emerged as promising optoelectronic devices due to their high speed
and eﬃcient modulation that is controllable through electrostatic gating. In
particular, optical modulation in the mid-infrared region has attracted
considerable interest for applications in biosensing, imaging, communication,
and computing. However, the scalability of metasurfaces poses a challenge as
typical fabrication pathways are not compatible with complementary
metal-oxide-semiconductor (CMOS) technology. In this work, a tunable
graphene-metasurface absorber is presented that integrates a
metal-dielectric-metal optical cavity with a graphene layer. Stable performance
in ambient conditions is achieved by the incorporation of an ultrathin Al2O3
capping layer. This barrier layer prevents direct contact between the metallic
antennas and the graphene layer, which results in a large on/oﬀratio. For a
gold metasurface, the creation of an optical cavity strongly enhances the
modulation depth of the reﬂectance between 7 µm to 8 µm from 11% to 47%.
By replacing gold with aluminum, a cost-eﬀective material employed in
foundry processes, a comparable maximum modulation depth of 49% is
obtained. These results open a new pathway for the integration of tunable
graphene–metal hybrid metasurfaces with CMOS-compatible technologies,
facilitating a scalable production of mid-infrared modulators.

A graphene ﬁeld eﬀect transistor (GFET) is an ideal plat-
form for investigating tunable mid-infrared metasurfaces, be-
cause of its ability to control resonances through electrostatic
gating,[33–35] chemical doping,[36] and optical pumping.[16,18] Fur-
thermore, it has been demonstrated that the plasmonic enhance-
ment of the light-graphene interaction leads to an increased sen-
sitivity/tunability of the device. Zhu et al.[22] demonstrated the
ability to detect glucose down to 200 pm (36 pg mL−1) by employ-
ing a graphene–metal nanoantenna hybrid metasuface. Dabidian
et al.[37] proposed the concept of electrical modulation of the in-
tensity of reﬂected light with a graphene-Fano resonance hybrid
metasurface. In our previous work, we demonstrated that an ul-
trathin Al2O3 barrier layer can enhance the tuning range of the
mid-infrared resonance of the tunable metasurface based on a
GFET by reducing the electrical coupling between the metal and
graphene.[13]
The majority of previous studies made use of noble met-
als, such as gold (Au) and silver (Ag), which are incompati-
ble with CMOS technology and increase fabrication costs, thus
limiting the potential for broad application. This problem can
be solved with the use of low-cost and CMOS-compatible ma-
terials. Common CMOS-compatible materials are silicon, ger-
manium, silicon dioxide (SiO2), silicon nitride (Si3N4), alu-
mina (Al2O3), used as gate dielectrics, and certain metals such
as aluminum (Al), tungsten, or copper, which are employed
in interconnects.[38–40] A straightforward approach to achieving
CMOS-compatible metasurfaces is the use of silicon-based di-
electric metasurfaces as an alternative to lossy plasmonic struc-
tures. In 2012, Kuznetsov et al. demonstrated that silicon nanos-
tructures can support strong magnetic resonances, laying the
foundation for high-index dielectric metasurfaces.[41] To lever-
age the extreme light conﬁnement of metallic metasurfaces,
researchers also explored CMOS-compatible plasmonic materi-
als. Knight et al. investigated the plasmonic properties of alu-
minum nanorod antennas.[45] Al, a common CMOS-compatible
metal, was later demonstrated to exhibit plasmonic properties
similar to gold and even outperform it in transformation optics
applications.[46,47]
Before replacing Au with Al in plasmonic applications, two
main trade-oﬀs must be considered: optical losses and fabrication
challenges. Al exhibits higher optical losses than Au in the visi-
ble and near-infrared range due to strong interband transitions
around 1.5 eV (≈800 nm).[42,43] However, in the mid-infrared
range, Al experiences lower losses, making it more comparable
to Au.[44] Unlike Au, Al supports plasmonic resonances in the
ultraviolet (UV) range, where Au suﬀers from strong interband
absorption.[45] While Ag also performs well in the UV region, its
susceptibility to oxidation rapidly degrades its plasmonic prop-
erties. In contrast, Al forms a stable native oxide layer (Al2O3),
which protects the metal from further oxidation over time.[46]
Fabrication challenges arise due to the demand for precisely fab-
ricating well-deﬁned Al nanostructures to optimize plasmonic
properties.[47] Al’s processing conditions are well-established in
CMOS-compatible fabrication, making it more scalable and cost-
eﬀective than Au.[48]
Despite extensive investigations of metallic and dielectric
metasurfaces, the integration of CMOS-compatible materials
with tunable metasurfaces, particularly in combination with 2D
materials like graphene, remains a challenge. This is due to two
main factors. Firstly, a good substrate must have nanoscale sur-
face smoothness to assure a high graphene transfer success rate
and minimize the number of charge traps, while common per-
fect absorbers metal-dielectric-metal structures, including Fabry-
Perot (FP) resonators, often exhibit a high surface roughness due
to lattice mismatches between the layers. Secondly, many studies
rely on graphene exfoliation or the direct ﬁshing technique,[49,50]
which is not compatible with large-scale fabrication.
In this study, we present an electrically tunable metasurface ab-
sorber that is fully compatible with CMOS fabrication processes.
A bipolar operation of the optical modulation is realized through
graphene’s Fermi level tuning in a ﬁeld eﬀect transistor architec-
ture, as illustrated in Figure 1. Figure 1b illustrates the modu-
lation principle: as the charge carrier concentration in graphene
(electrons or holes) increases, the resonance frequency shifts to-
ward the blue. The integration of a FP cavity enhances the light
conﬁnement in the metasurface, enabling signiﬁcant spectral in-
tensity changes and facilitating an “OFF” to “ON” switching be-
havior. Additionally, incorporation of a 15 nm Si3N4 interlayer re-
duces the surface roughness of the Al2O3, making it suitable for
graphene transfer. An additional uniform 3 nm insulating Al2O3
ﬁlm on top of the graphene acts as a barrier and encapsulation
layer. The electrical transport characteristics provide evidence for
the device’s high on/oﬀcurrent ratio and stability in ambient con-
ditions. This unique fabrication protocol results in an enhanced
reﬂectance modulation depth, showcasing the device’s potential
as a high-eﬃciency CMOS-compatible mid-infrared modulator.
2. Results and Discussion
2.1. Design of a CMOS-Compatible Perfect Absorption
Metasurface
The metasurface is designed to be a modulator that operates
in the mid-infrared range of the EM spectrum. The design is
shown schematically in Figure 2a,c, with an FP cavity and Al
nanoantenna array on top. The design has two major advantages
over traditional metamaterial perfect absorbers. First, the metal-
dielectric-metal structure works as an asymmetric FP resonator,
which contains a partially reﬂecting mirror (the nanoantenna ar-
rays) and a fully reﬂecting back mirror (the bottom Cu ﬁlm). In
asymmetric FP resonators, only the electric resonance needs to
be considered as the resonance is governed by the constructive
interference of light between the two reﬂective surfaces. As a re-
sult, the absorption increases and the design is much easier com-
pared to traditional metamaterials that combine an electric and
a magnetic resonance.[51–53] Second, the use of Cu and Al, which
are commonly employed in CMOS processes, as substitutes for
Au in traditional metasurfaces, enables a straightforward future
integration into large-scale industrial fabrication.
To understand the underlying mechanism that causes the in-
creased absorption, we simulated the electric ﬁeld distribution
within the metasurface for a device with 30 nm thick Al nanoan-
tennas. The polarization of the incident light is aligned with the
antennas’ long axes to excite the antenna dipole mode. Figure 2b
shows the ﬁeld enhancement in the x-y plane of the nanogap and
the dipole nature of the resonance. Figure 2d depicts the simu-
lation results for the x-z plane, showing that most of the ﬁeld is
conﬁned within the nanogaps between adjacent antennas rather

Figure 1. Working principle of the mid-infrared modulator. a) Schematic representation of the GFET capable of switching the intensity of the free-space
reﬂected light. The optical resonator is designed as a FP cavity, composed of the Al nanoantenna array, dielectric layers (Al2O3 and Si3N4), and a bottom
Cu mirror. The nanoanntennas and graphene are physically separated by an ultrathin Al2O3 layer. b) Schematic representation of the modulation principle
based on the back gate voltage-induced change of graphene’s charge carrier density. The resonance frequency 𝜔0 is recorded when the back-gate voltage
is at the charge neutrality point (CNP), while resonance frequencies 𝜔1 and 𝜔2 are shifted due to the bias-voltage induced hole and electron charge

than in the interior of the cavity. The over 200-fold enhancement
of the Ez ﬁeld results from the combined eﬀects of light con-
ﬁnement by the paired antennas and the FP resonator. Without
the Cu back mirror the maximal ﬁeld enhancement factor is less
than 100. The maximum ﬁeld intensity enhancement is approx-
imately one hundred thousand, which is an order of magnitude
higher than without a metallic back plate.[13] Despite aluminum’s
slightly higher losses in the mid-infrared region than Au, a large
ﬁeld enhancement is still evident within the nanogap between
the Al antennas.
The perfect absorption of light in the FP resonator can be ex-
plained by interference theory, which is governed by multiple re-
ﬂections between the two mirrors.[54] The reﬂectance of the meta-
surface results from the superposition of these reﬂections within
the resonating cavity, and can become zero when the roundtrip
phase accumulation enables destructive interference, known as
the critical coupling condition. The phase accumulation is a func-
tion of the relative dielectric thickness ndH0∕𝜆0, where nd is the
refraction index of the dielectric, H0 its thickness, and 𝜆0 the
wavelength of the free space light. To understand the interplay be-
tween the various constituents of the multiparameter space that
leads to perfect absorption, we performed a parametric sweep of
reﬂectance R as a function of wavelength for both the length of
the antennas and the thickness of the Al2O3 layer. As shown in
Figure 2e, with H0 exceeding 300 nm, perfect absorption is ob-
served between 7.9 and 8.4 μm. If the thickness of the dielec-
tric layer is further increased, perfect absorption shifts to longer
wavelengths, accompanied by a reduction in the quality factor
(Q-factor). The redshift occurs because longer wavelengths are
required to satisfy the critical coupling condition when the di-
electric cavity thickness is increased. The decrease in the Q-factor
is attributed to increased internal losses in the thicker dielectric
layer, which leads to a larger absorption. To achieve a balance be-
tween optimal absorption and a high Q-factor, a H0 = 300 nm
Al2O3 layer was selected. This thickness provides the best com-
promise for absorption eﬃciency in the desired wavelength re-
gion. To validate the eﬀective absorption of the 300 nm thick
Al2O3 layer, simulations were conducted with varying antenna
lengths (Figure 2f), showing a reasonable scaling of the perfect
absorption wavelengths as the antenna lengths increase.
Though the natural oxide layer on Al antennas is only a few
nanometers, its thickness can be increased with high tempera-
ture annealing.[56] Figure 2g examines the impact of a naturally
formed oxide layer on the stability of Al antennas by simulating
the reﬂectance for ultrathin Al2O3 layers ranging from 0 nm to
16 nm in 1 nm increments. The results indicate that a native ox-
ide layer thinner than 10 nm has a negligible eﬀect on the res-
onance behavior, ensuring that the antenna’s performance re-
mains stable and reproducible for MIR applications. This simu-
lation suggests that the metasurface maintains its characteristics
even under small variations in the degree of oxidation.
2.2. Characterization of the CMOS-Compatible Metasurface
Since the performance of a perfect absorber metasurface is sub-
ject to small variations in the material properties, fabrication im-
perfections, and the surface roughness, it is essential to conﬁrm
the predictions of the ﬁnite element simulations presented in
Figure 2. Therefore, before investigating the electric tunability of
the metasurface, we measured the behavior of the device with a
300 nm Al2O3 layer without applying a back-gate voltage. How-
ever, directly depositing a 300 nm Al2O3 layer onto a metal sub-
strate typically leads to signiﬁcant surface roughness. To address
this, a 15 nm Si3N4 interlayer was integrated in the metasurface
design. This resulted in a dielectric-metal substrate with an RMS
roughness of approximately 0.6 nm, providing an ideal surface
for high-quality graphene transfer. The detailed substrate prepa-
ration and sample fabrication is described in the Experimental
section.

A scanning electron microscope (SEM) image of the device is
shown in Figure 3a, with a zoom on the gap between two paired
antennas (Figure 3b). It is known that the resonance wavelength
of metasurfaces scales roughly linear with the antenna length at
mid-infrared or longer wavelengths.[55] To map the scaling behav-
ior of the mid-infrared metasurfaces, we fabricated samples with
diﬀerent antenna lengths (L from 0.8 to 2.4 μm). This is done for
a ﬁxed antenna gap size of 20 nm and for a vertical period 2.0 μm.
The resulting spectra, measured with Fourier-transform infrared
spectroscopy (FTIR), are presented in Figure 3c. The arrow indi-
cates the observed red shift with increasing antenna lengths. The
overall experimental resonance wavelengths agree well with the
FDTD simulations (Figure 2f); however, the measured reﬂection
minima are about 10% higher than the simulation predictions.

The main reason for this deviation is that the additional optical
losses from the deposition of the aluminum and dielectric layers
were not considered in the simulation, which alters the critical
coupling conditions.
Al is both cost-eﬀective and highly stable due to its self-
limiting native oxide layer, which prevents further oxidation and
shields the surface from contaminants, ensuring long-term de-
vice stability.[46] To further assess the impact of temperature and
humidity ﬂuctuations, thermal annealing was performed on the
devices at 100 °C and 300 °C for 1 h under ambient conditions.
The extracted resonance wavelengths are presented in Figure 3d,
showing a linear shift in resonance wavelength with increasing
antenna length. This trend enables precise tuning of the reso-
nance wavelength by simply adjusting the antenna length. No-
tably, annealing at 100 °C causes a minimal resonance shift,
whereas annealing at 300 °C results in a slight blueshift of ap-
proximately 150 nm. This blueshift likely arises from a compe-
tition between weak oxidation of Al and the reduction of grain
boundaries.[56] The maximum absorption remains largely un-
changed across the diﬀerent annealing temperatures, suggest-
ing that the device is compatible with standard CMOS processing
temperatures (measured spectra shown in Figure S4, Supporting
Information).
2.3. Back-Gate Control of CMOS-Compatible Metasurface-GFET
Device
To investigate the tunability of the designed CMOS-compatible
metasurface, we integrated the proposed multilayer structure and
the GFET architecture (Figure 4a). Bonding pads, traditionally
made from Au, were made with Al to be CMOS-compatible, and
Pd is used as an interlayer on top of graphene to reduce the con-
tact resistance. The cross-section view of the device in Figure 4b
also shows the electrical connections. The source-drain current
Isd is applied to the graphene channel. Together with the two volt-
age probes they allow to measure the graphene sheet resistance.
Considering the dimensions of the sheet (Figure 4c), the sheet
resistivity can be calculated as 𝜌Sheet = WΔV∕LIsd , where ΔV is
the measured voltage between the middle contacts and W and
L are the width (90 μm) and the length (50 μm) of the probed
area, respectively. The back-gate voltage is applied to the Cu layer
through the p++ Si substrate and controls the graphene’s Fermi
level position. A 3 nm Al2O3 layer is deposited with precursor-
based soaking and atomic layer deposition (ALD) between the
single layer graphene and the Al antennas. This ultrathin insulat-
ing layer prevents direct graphene–metal contact,[13] which could
cause a decrease in the on/oﬀcurrent ratio.

The Al2O3 layer that is grown over the entire device prevents
the adsorption and desorption of molecules in the ambient
(Figure 4d), is crucial to obtain a stable ﬁeld eﬀect character-
istic upon sweeping the voltage. Figure 4f shows the extracted
CNP voltage and resistivity at the CNP—these parameters vary
slightly in the ﬁrst 5 cycles and then stabilize in the later 5 cycles,
a common sign of the stabilization process. The stable CNP
voltage is about 50 V. Its diﬀerence from zero is likely the result
of the trapped charges at the Al2O3/graphene interface.[57] The
relatively high CNP voltage may be decreased in future work
by two methods. First, improving the interface quality can shift
the CNP voltage back to 0 V. For example, replacing Al2O3 with
van der Waals (vdW) materials such as hexagonal boron nitride
(h-BN) or transition metal dichalcogenides (TMDs) provides a

dangling-bond-free surface, mitigating charge traps and low-
ering the CNP voltage.[58–60] Second, reducing the equivalent
oxide thickness (EOT) of GFETs by using a thin high-k top-gate
dielectric lowers the operational voltage.[61,62] However, this op-
tion requires a double-layer graphene conﬁguration[63–65] since
conventional metal gates are not transparent to infrared light.
In our bottom-gate design, replacing the SiO2 gating dielectric
layer with Al2O3 enables lowering operational voltages due to the
increased dielectric constant, which rises from 3.9 to 9. This al-
lows to achieve a higher on/oﬀcurrent ratio with the same op-
eration voltage.[66,67] To demonstrate this idea, we measured the
drain-source current Isd as a function of the gate bias VG for drain-
source voltages (Vsd) from -0.5 to 0.5 V changed in steps of 0.25 V
(Figure 4e). The Isd increases from 53 μA (VG = 60 V) to 262 μA
(VG = -80 V) at a Vsd of 0.5 V, indicating that the charge carrier
concentration in graphene can be eﬃciently modulated by the
applied back-gate voltage.
2.4. Reﬂectance Modulation of CMOS-Compatible
Metal-Graphene Metasurface
The
reﬂectance
modulation
of
the
CMOS-compatible
metasurface-GFET device was studied with an FTIR microscope.
Figure 5a,b shows the spectra under diﬀerent back-gate voltages
for devices with the FP cavity metal antennas/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu,
for metal antennas made of Au and Al, respectively. To evaluate
the performance of the fabricated modulator, we conducted
reference measurements of the Au antennas without the FP
cavity (on SiO2/p-Si). Figure 5c represents the spectra under
diﬀerent back-gate voltages for the Au antennas/SiO2/p-Si
reference device. Notably, the bandwidth of the resonance is
largely decreased due to the enhanced light conﬁnement in the
cavity, which explains the enhanced modulation ability discussed
further in the text.
The extracted resonance wavelengths at various back-gate volt-
ages are plotted in Figure 5d–f (black squares). The devices
have their CNPs at back-gate voltage of 60, 40, and 50 V, allow-
ing for both p-doped and n-doped GFET operation. As seen in
Figure 5d, the reﬂectance spectra of the Au antennas/SiO2/p-
Si device exhibit a blue shift of 0.80 μm when the back-gate
voltage is decreased from 60 to -80 V. In contrast, the Al
antennas/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu device yields a smaller blue shift of
0.40 μm when the back-gate voltage is decreased from 40 to -
80 V (Figure 5e). The reference sample provides a resonance
wavelength tuning of 0.56 μm (Figure 5f). The applied voltage in
the reference sample is ±100 V instead of ±80 V to compensate
for the decreased charge carrier concentration resulting from the
lower dielectric constant of SiO2 compared to Al2O3. The trends
of resonance wavelength tuning follow changes in graphene’s re-
sistivity. Notably, the three devices have diﬀerent initial doping
levels, which aﬀect the CNP and consequently inﬂuence the tun-
ing range of the resonance wavelength with the backgate voltage.
Those variations are likely related to the ALD growth processes of
Al2O3, which is known to result in a dielectric layer with charged
defects. Those have an unpredictable inﬂuence on the value of
the CNP voltage.
To evaluate the device’s performance as a mid-infrared mod-
ulator, the modulation depth (MD) was used as a ﬁgure of
merit. It is deﬁned as MD(𝜆) = |ΔR(𝜆)| ∕max[(Ron(𝜆); Roﬀ(𝜆))] ×
100%,[13,37,68] where RON(𝜆) and ROFF(𝜆) represent the reﬂectance
values at the chosen wavelengths in the ON and OFF states, re-
spectively. Similar to the convention presented in Figure 1a, the
ON state represent the reﬂectance value for the operating volt-
age away from the CNP, while the OFF state is recorded with the
back-gate voltage equal to the CNP, i.e., the state corresponding
to the lowest graphene conductance. Figure 5g (blue line) depicts
the measured MD of the Au antennas/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu device
as a function of wavelength in the p-doped state of graphene,
reaching two maxima at 7.2 μm and 8.1 μm, with a maximum
MD of ≈47%. In Figure 5d, the p (n)-doped region of graphene
is shaded in blue (red), i.e., when VG is smaller (larger) than
60 V. Similarly, Figure 5h shows the MD determined for the
Al antennas/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu metasurface, reaching its highest
values of ≈49% at 7.3 and 8.0 μm. The p and n doped region
of graphene in this device are marked in a similar manner
in Figure 5e as was done for Au antennas/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu in
Figure 5d. Due to the positive CNP in both Au and Al devices,
the MD is lower in the n-doped state of graphene for the in-
vestigated back-gate voltage range. Although the spectral tuning
range of the Au antennas/SiO2/p-Si metasurface reference de-
vice (Figure 5f) is only slightly less that of the devices with FP
resonator (Figure 5d,e), its maximum MD is much smaller. This
indicates that the FP cavity is beneﬁcial for increasing the optical
modulation capability.
To benchmark the performance of the fabricated metasurface
with the state-of-the-art devices presented in the literatures, a
comparison with various hybrid metasurfaces is made in Table 1.
The table contains information about the metasurface design, the
order of the layers, the maximum MD, whether the device has
an encapsulation layer and is CMOS-compatible, and the modu-
lation eﬃciency. Early studies were devoted to the realization of
the perfect absorption by incorporating antennas of diﬀerent res-
onance mechanisms into a FP resonator, such as waveguide-type
resonance, Fano resonance and even coupling between radiation
and graphene plasmonic modes.[11,37,69] Those coupling mecha-
nisms allow to reach nearly perfect absorption, but at the cost of
complex designs and challenges for CMOS processes. More re-
cent work focused on the use of dielectric material to increase
the quality factor of the resonance and achieve higher MD.[68,70]
For example, by incorporating the guided resonance of a pho-
tonic crystal slab into graphene/h-BN layers and using dielectric-
metal layers to achieve the perfect absorption, a maximum MD
of 99.98% could be achieved.[68]
The devices reported in the abovementioned works did not
have an encapsulation layer, which hampers long term reliability.
Furthermore, designs based on complex metasurfaces increase
the cost of fabrication and adaptation ability. In contrast, the
metasurface proposed in the current work has a 3 nm insulating
Al2O3 layer, acting both as a barrier and encapsulation layer.
With this thin layer a stable GFET device working in ambient
conditions was obtained, it was also shown that substituting the
Au antennas with CMOS-compatible Al ones, does not aﬀect
the maximum MD, being 47% for Au and 49% for Al. This
implies that the Al antennas graphene/Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu device
can be a general solution for mid-infrared modulators based
on a graphene CMOS-compatible metasurface absorber. The
maximum MD can be further increased to ≈100% when near

Figure 2e has shown that increasing H0 beyond 300 nm facili-
tates perfect absorption; however, a greater thickness also raises
the operational voltage and reduces eﬃciency, which is deﬁned as
the maximum MD divided by the applied voltage.[71,72] Addition-
ally, the MD can be improved by increasing the gate tunability of
graphene. For example, a double-layer graphene conﬁguration
with a thin high-k dielectric top gate enables a higher charge
carrier concentration in the “ON” state, leading to increased
graphene absorption and a signiﬁcantly larger MD.[63–65] Based
on this eﬃciency metric, the devices with Au and Al anten-
nas in this work has eﬃciencies of 0.59%/V and 0.61%/V,
respectively— outperforming most devices reported in litera-
ture, except for the waveguide antenna device, which achieves an
eﬃciency of 1.19%/V. The high eﬃciency is primarily attributed
to the enhanced light–graphene interaction in the nanogaps
of the V-shaped paired antennas. This design increases the
interaction volume, enhances absorption, and ultimately enables
a higher maximum modulation depth under the same applied
voltage.[11]
3. Conclusions
A CMOS-compatible tunable graphene-based mid-infrared meta-
surface absorber was designed and fabricated. The deposition
of an ultrathin 3 nm Al2O3 layer, which fully encapsulates the
graphene, prevents the decrease in gate tunability over time and
minimizes the adsorption of molecules during the device’s opera-
tion in the ambient. The electrical transfer characteristics validate
the device’s high on/oﬀcurrent ratio and stability.
By incorporating a CMOS-compatible metasurface consist-
ing of Al antennas on a FP cavity into the graphene ﬁeld-
eﬀect transistor architecture, we realized the electrically tun-
able metasurface with a modulation depth up to 49%. These
results emphasize the potential for the design and construc-
tion of high-performance mid-infrared modulator. The proposed
CMOS-compatible procedure provides guidelines for the devel-
opment of 2D material-based optoelectronics and oﬀers adapt-
ability for advanced applications, such as spatial light modulators
for single-pixel imaging[32,74] and high resolution biosensing.[75]
Future work may focus on integrating wafer-level lithography and
packaging to replace E-beam lithography, further increase the
scalability, and reduce the fabrication costs.
4. Experimental Section
Device Fabrication and Characterization—Simulation:
A 3D ﬁnite-
diﬀerence time-domain (3D-FDTD) solver (Lumerical Solutions, Inc.) was
employed to calculate the localized ﬁeld enhancement and the reﬂectance
spectra of the CMOS-compatible metasurfaces. The optical response of
graphene was modeled using the surface conductivity approach, which
accounts for its permittivity as a 2D material. To ensure accurate spatial
resolution, the mesh size was set at 0.5 nm × 0.5 nm × 0.5 nm. The
dielectric properties of aluminum, aluminum oxide, silicon nitride, and
the copper substrate were deﬁned using the Palik model. A perfectly
matched layer (PML) boundary condition with 64 layers was applied
along the z-axis to minimize reﬂection artifacts, while periodic and
symmetric boundary conditions were imposed along the x- and y-axes,
respectively.
Graphene was grown using a wafer-scale epitaxial process as described
in previous work.[76,77] The PMMA-supported graphene layer was trans-
ferred onto the Al2O3 (300 nm) /Si3N4 (15 nm) /Cu (250 nm) on a p++-
doped Si substrate using the procedure described in Section SI of the Sup-
porting Information.
To achieve the desired resonance properties, it is crucial to realize high
resolution and accurate fabrication. In contrast to the typically applied
room temperature development process after E-beam lithography with the
use of PMMA, cold development is employed in this study to increase
the resolution. This way antenna arrays with sharper edges and less di-
mensional variations were obtained (see details in Section SI, Support-
ing Information). Following the PMMA development, Au nanoantenna ar-
rays were added by thermal evaporation. The antennas consist of a 30 nm
thick Au layer and a 5 nm Pd adhesion layer. The Al nanoantenna arrays of
30 nm thickness were patterned using e-beam evaporation (Pfeiﬀer PLS
580 unit with base pressure of 10−5 mbar). The graphene was then pat-
terned with the use of electron beam lithography (EBL), and reactive ion
etching was used to remove excess graphene, resulting in a rectangu-
lar graphene sheet. The source and drain electrodes were patterned us-
ing a similar procedure, followed by e-beam evaporation of a 20 nm Pd
layer. A low-temperature trimethylaluminum (TMA-H2O) physiosorbed-
precursor-assisted ALD process was utilized in a 300 mm ALD system
(Polygon8300, ASM) to promote precursor adsorption onto the non-
reactive graphene surface, forming a 1 nm Al2O3 interfacial layer.[78] Sub-
sequently, a 2 nm Al2O3 layer was deposited using a cyclic TMA-H2O ALD
process in another 300 mm ALD system (XP4, ASM). BCl3 and Cl2 gas-
based ICP etching was employed to remove the excessive Al2O3 from the
Pd top layer, followed by the deposition of a 200 nm Al layer for electri-
cal contacts. Finally, electrical transport properties were determined with
a Keithley 2450A nanovoltmeter under a DC current of 1 μA with the back-
gate voltage applied from a Keithley 2400 voltage source.
Realization of a Substrate for Graphene Layer Transfer with Nanoscopic
Surface Roughness:
The surface roughness is one of the major obstacles
in integrating the FP cavity with graphene.[79–81] Low surface roughness is
essential for creating a tunable graphene-metal perfect absorber because
the roughness of the support directly impacts graphene’s electrical and
optical properties. High roughness can also lead to poor transfer. The FP
cavity requires a thick ALD layer to be grown on a metal substrate, which

ever, metals often have low surface energy, causing poor interaction with
the ALD precursors. As a result, nucleation tends to lead to the forma-
tion of clusters or islands, which increases the surface roughness.[82,83]
An eﬀective solution is the introduction of a thin seeding layer. A seeding
layer typically has higher surface energy, which promotes better nucleation
of the ALD ﬁlm, resulting in a more uniform deposition and reducing the
surface roughness.[84]
Here we use a 15 nm Si3N4 seeding layer due to its high surface energy,
good adhesion properties and thermal stability.[85] The morphology of the
deposited dielectric ﬁlms was investigated with Atomic Force Microscopy
(AFM). Figure 6 depicts tapping mode topographic images of the sam-
ples, both without (Figure 6a) and with the Si3N4 interlayer (Figure 6b).
These images show that the particle size decreased from 59 ± 5 to 2.1
± 0.1 nm, and the root mean square (RMS) roughness reduced from 4.9
± 0.9 to 0.64 ± 0.03 nm by the presence of the Si3N4 interlayer. To verify the
substrate’s suitability for graphene transfer, the Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu substrate
was used for transferring CVD graphene. Figure 6e,f shows AFM results
after a successful graphene transfer on the Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu substrate and
subsequent cleaning to remove PMMA residuals. The AFM image of the
acetone-treated substrate (Figure 6e) shows that most of the PMMA was
removed, though some remnants can still be observed. In contrast, H2
plasma treatment (Figure 6f) eﬀectively removed most of the PMMA, pro-
viding the possibility for the subsequent growth of a uniform and ultrathin
Al2O3 barrier layer.
Optical Modulation Characterization:
In the optical modulation exper-
iment, samples were characterized under ambient conditions using an
FTIR spectrometer (Bruker Vertex 80v + Hyperion 2000) with a spectral
resolution of 1 cm−1. A 60 μm × 60 μm aperture in the mid-infrared mi-
croscope was employed to ensure a good signal-to-noise ratio and to avoid
saturation. The incident light was linearly polarized along the long axis of
the nanoantennas, and the reﬂected light was collected with a cooled mer-
cury cadmium telluride detector. The reﬂectance spectra were normalized
to a 200 nm thick gold ﬁlm on the same Al2O3/Si3N4/Cu substrate.
